title: EST Literacy Test 2: Reading
kicker: American Diploma · EST I · Literacy Test 2
summary: Every reading skill on the test, a method and pacing plan for 52 questions in 65 minutes, and an original passage with ten practice questions.

blocks.text: Literacy Test 2 is the **Reading** part of EST I. You read texts — stories, articles, arguments, sometimes with a table or a second text — and answer questions about what they say, what they suggest and how they are built. This guide explains each skill, gives you a reading method and a pacing plan, and ends with a full original passage and ten questions.
What this test tests

As published by schools, Literacy Test 2 has **52 multiple-choice questions in 65 minutes**. Every question has four choices. The answer is always supported by the text — never by your outside knowledge or opinion.

blocks.title: Important
blocks.text: These figures are as published by schools; check the latest official EST candidate guide on est.moe.gov.eg before your test. The exact passage lengths and question order are not given in the published school information, so practise both short texts (SAT style) and long passages (ACT style) on this site.

rows: "Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?"
Sum up the whole text in one sentence before you look at the choices.
Go back to the lines; the answer is stated, often in different words.
"It can most reasonably be inferred that…"
Choose what must be true from the text — the smallest safe step.
"As used in line X, the word … most nearly means"
Cover the word, put in your own word, then match. The common meaning is often the trap.
"The main purpose of the third paragraph is to…"
Ask: why did the writer put this here? Use verbs: introduce, explain, contrast, illustrate, conclude.
"Which quotation best supports the claim that…?"
The right quotation proves the exact claim, not just the topic.
"Which choice uses data from the table to support…?"
Check the numbers AND that they prove the stated point.
"How would the author of Text 2 respond to…?"
Find each author's main view, then the point where they agree or disagree.

blocks.text: Strategy: 52 questions in 65 minutes

65 ÷ 52 = **1.25 minutes = 75 seconds per question**, and this time includes reading the passages. If a passage has several questions, the reading time is shared between them, so a good first read saves time on every question that follows.

rows: Question 52 finished — 2 minutes to check flagged questions

blocks.text: The reading method, step by step

items: **Read the introduction line** (if there is one): who wrote it, when, about what.
**Read the passage once, actively.** After each paragraph, write two or three words on your scrap paper: "problem", "survey results", "warning".
**After the passage, say the main idea in one sentence** — before you look at any question.
**Read the question and find the line** it refers to. Read a little before and after.
**Answer in your own words first**, then look for the choice that matches.
**Eliminate by trap type:** too broad, too narrow, too extreme, opposite, true but not the answer, off-topic.
**Prove it.** Point to the words in the text that support your choice. If you cannot point, it is probably wrong.

blocks.title: القاعدة الذهبية في الـ Reading
blocks.text: الإجابة الصح دايمًا موجودة في النص — مش في معلوماتك ولا رأيك. قبل ما تختار، اسأل نفسك: أقدر أشاور على الكلام اللي في النص اللي يثبت الإجابة دي؟ لو مش قادر، غالبًا الإجابة غلط.
Worked examples

**Example 1 (vocabulary in context).** Text: "The coach was famous for her economy with words: after a win she said 'Good,' and after a loss she said nothing at all." Question: As used in the text, "economy" most nearly means A) wealth B) careful, limited use C) business system D) low price

**Answer: B.** She uses very few words, so "economy" means careful, limited use. **A** and **C** are the common meanings of "economy" — the classic vocabulary trap. **D** belongs to shopping ("economy class"), not to speech.

**Example 2 (inference).** Text: "By the time Karim reached the platform, the train doors were closing. He stopped running, checked the board, and sat down on a bench with his book." Question: What can most reasonably be inferred about Karim? A) He was angry with the driver. B) He decided to wait for a later train. C) He had missed his train many times before. D) He did not want to travel at all.

**Answer: B.** He checks the board and sits down to read — he is waiting for the next train. **A** invents an emotion. **C** is not supported ("many times" is extreme). **D** contradicts his running to catch the train.
**Example 3 (data).** A student uses this table to support the claim "The chess club grew more than any other club."

Which choice best supports the claim? A) Drama had the most members in 2024. B) Chess grew by 12 members, while robotics grew by 9 and drama lost one. C) Robotics almost doubled its membership. D) Chess had 30 members in 2025.
**Answer: B.** Only B compares the growth of all clubs. **A** is true but about drama. **C** is true but supports a different claim. **D** gives one number with no comparison — half the evidence.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Too extreme:** always, never, all, completely — the text rarely says this.
**Too broad / too narrow:** a main idea choice that covers more than the text, or only one paragraph.
**True but not the answer:** a fact from the passage that does not answer this question.
**Opposite:** uses the passage's words but reverses the meaning.
**Common meaning:** in vocabulary questions, the everyday meaning of the word is often wrong in context.
**Half the data:** a correct number that does not prove the comparison the question asks for.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: One active read per passage; note the main idea of each paragraph in two or three words.
Answer in your own words before reading the choices.
Find the line, then prove your choice with words from the text.
Checkpoints: Q13 at 16 min, Q26 at 32, Q39 at 48.
Flag and move on after about 90 seconds on one question.

items: الإجابة اللي فيها كلمات قوية زي always أو never غالبًا غلط.
إجابة صح في النص بس مش بتجاوب على السؤال = فخ.
في أسئلة معنى الكلمة: المعنى المشهور للكلمة غالبًا مش هو المقصود.

blocks.text: Practice
Read the passage once using the method above, then answer the ten questions. The last question adds a short second text. Untimed — but note how long you take: about 12–13 minutes would be on pace.

blocks.title: Literacy 2 practice: The Missing Readers
blocks.intro: One passage with a table, 10 questions. The answer is always in the text.

questions.p:
The Missing Readers
Every September, our school librarian, Mr. Hany, posts the borrowing figures from the previous year on the board outside the library. Last year the numbers looked worse than ever, and he asked my Grade 11 class a simple question: if students are not borrowing books, what are they reading instead?
Most of us assumed we already knew the answer. Teenagers, the familiar story goes, have abandoned reading for short videos. Our first idea was simply to count how many hours students spent on their phones and declare the case closed. Mr. Hany suggested that we test the story rather than repeat it. "A good question," he said, "deserves a better answer than the one you brought into the room."
So we designed a survey. Over two weeks, 120 students from Grades 9 to 12 answered questions about what they had read in the previous seven days, where they had found it, and why they had chosen it. Before we began, a small group of teachers tried the questions, and we rewrote two that they found confusing. We were careful to define reading broadly: novels and textbooks counted, but so did news articles, online stories, comics and long messages from friends. Several of us argued that this definition was too generous, since a message about homework is hardly literature. In the end we kept it, because we wanted to know how much students read before deciding whether what they read was "good enough".
The results surprised us. Almost every student reported reading something every day, and the average total was well over an hour. What had changed was not whether students read but where. Only a small share of reading time involved printed books, while the largest share took place on phones. Many students described following long online stories that were published in chapters, sometimes reading for an hour at night without thinking of it as reading at all. Several said they read news articles on the way to school, usually in short bursts of a few minutes. One Grade 10 student wrote that she "never reads", and then listed four serialised stories she was following.
The survey also suggested a reason for the fall in borrowing that none of us had predicted. When we asked students who had stopped using the library why they had stopped, the most common answer was not lack of interest but lack of time during the school day: the library's opening hours overlapped almost completely with lessons. In other words, part of the problem was a timetable, not a generation.
We should be cautious about these findings. Our sample came from one school, students reported their own habits, and people often remember their reading less accurately than they think. Still, the pattern was strong enough that Mr. Hany decided to act on it. This year the library opens for forty minutes after the final lesson, and a shelf near the door now holds printed copies of the serialised stories students recommended in the survey.
It is too early to say whether borrowing will recover. What has already changed is the way my classmates talk about the question. At the start of the project, we treated the falling numbers as a verdict on our generation. By the end, we saw them as a clue, and a clue is something you can follow. Mr. Hany says that is the real reason he asked us: not to rescue the library, but to see what happens when students investigate a claim about themselves instead of accepting it. A few of us have even started borrowing again, if only to see what the new shelf holds.
Table: Share of reported reading time by format (survey of 120 students)
Format | Share of reading time
Phone | 58%
Laptop or tablet | 21%
Printed books and magazines | 14%
Other | 7%
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
c: Teenagers have stopped reading because they prefer short videos.
School libraries should replace printed books with phones.
A class survey questioned a common belief about teenage reading and revealed a practical reason for falling library use.
Surveys are an unreliable way to study how students read.
questions.e: C covers the whole passage: the test of the "familiar story" and the timetable finding. A is the belief the passage questions (opposite); B is not suggested; D is too narrow — the writer mentions limits but still trusts the pattern.

questions.q: According to the passage, why did the class keep its broad definition of reading?
c: They wanted to measure how much students read before judging the quality of that reading.
Mr. Hany insisted that messages about homework were literature.
Students refused to answer questions about textbooks.
A narrow definition would have made the survey take longer than two weeks.
questions.e: Paragraph 3 says they kept it "because we wanted to know how much students read before deciding whether what they read was 'good enough'". B reverses a student's objection; C and D are never stated.

questions.q: As used in paragraph 3, "generous" most nearly means
c: kind
wealthy
careful
inclusive
questions.e: The students worried the definition included too many kinds of text, so "generous" means inclusive. "Kind" and "wealthy" are common meanings that do not fit; "careful" is unrelated.

questions.q: Based on the passage, what can most reasonably be inferred from the Grade 10 student's answer?
c: She did not answer the survey honestly.
Some students do not think of reading online stories as "reading".
She prefers printed books to online stories.
The survey questions were too difficult to understand.
questions.e: She says she "never reads" yet follows four stories, which supports the passage's point that students read "without thinking of it as reading". A is too extreme; C and D have no support.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the sentence "In other words, part of the problem was a timetable, not a generation" in paragraph 5?
c: To sum up a finding that moves the cause of falling borrowing from students' attitudes to a scheduling problem
To introduce a new argument against carrying out the survey
To criticise the librarian for choosing the opening hours
To give an example of how students read on their phones
questions.e: "In other words" signals a summary of the finding just described. B and C invent criticism; D refers to paragraph 4's topic, not this sentence.

questions.q: Which quotation best supports the claim that the writer recognises limits to the survey's findings?
c: "The results surprised us."
"Almost every student reported reading something every day"
"Our sample came from one school, students reported their own habits"
"a shelf near the door now holds printed copies"
questions.e: C names two weaknesses of the survey. A shows surprise, not limits; B is a finding; D describes an action taken afterwards.

Text 2 (a teacher's comment on the survey)
Students who say they read for an hour a day on their phones are not wrong, but much of that reading jumps quickly from one short piece to the next. Following a single long text for an hour builds a kind of attention that scrolling rarely does. Counting minutes alone may hide this difference.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the class's decision to define reading broadly and count minutes?
c: By agreeing that all kinds of reading build the same skills
By accepting that it shows how much students read but warning that it may not show what kind of reading they do
By arguing that the survey should have been about short videos
By claiming that students who read on phones are not telling the truth
questions.e: Text 2 says students "are not wrong" about their minutes but that counting minutes "may hide" a difference in attention. A is the opposite; C is off-topic; D contradicts "are not wrong".

blocks.title: Remember
items: Literacy Test 2 = Reading, 52 questions in 65 minutes as published by schools (check the official candidate guide): 75 seconds per question including reading.
Read actively once, note each paragraph's point, and state the main idea before the questions.
Answer in your own words, then match — and prove your choice with words from the text.
Watch for extreme, too broad, opposite and true-but-not-the-answer choices.
For data questions, the right choice proves the exact comparison asked for.
